S79.01.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account and session saving on (not the default for --no-session-persistence)
S79.01.note: How a session enters Managed mode is only implied by the error text (Switch to Managed with /model first); the exact step was not confirmed.
steps: Start the CLI with agi and sign in to a managed cloud account.
Type /model and pick a managed cloud model, so the session runs in Managed mode.
Type /route with no argument and read the Routing and Profiles lines.
Type /route auto, then send a normal prompt and look for the model named in the Auto route notice or the Routing set to message, to compare with Expected.

labels.text: Model to use (must match the shared model catalog/provider metadata)

steps: Type /model in the chat to open the model picker.
Pick a model row and press Enter.
Type a message and check the reply and the model shown in the status or banner.
Compare with Expected: the request should run on the chosen model.

S79.04.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account and session saving on
S79.04.note: The quality profile maps to the server selection auto-premium; the task-specific premium choice for coding and reasoning is made by the registry, not visible on its own.
steps: Start with a managed cloud account and session saving on, as in S79.01.
Type /route quality.
Read the line Routing set to ... for the quality profile; the label comes from the server catalog.
Send a coding or reasoning prompt and check the model named in the reply or notice.

S79.05.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account and session saving on
S79.05.note: Speed maps to the auto-economy selection with speed-first set; the speed-first effect itself is not shown on screen.
steps: Start with a managed cloud account and session saving on.
Type /route speed.
Read the Routing set to message, which shows the speed profile label from the server.
Send a prompt and compare the response speed and model with Expected.

S79.06.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account and session saving on
steps: Start with a managed cloud account and session saving on.
Type /route quality.
Read the Routing set to message.
Send a prompt and compare the chosen model with Expected.

S79.07.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account and session saving on
S79.07.note: Cost maps to the auto-economy selection; the cheapest-route ranking is not shown on screen.
steps: Start with a managed cloud account and session saving on.
Type /route cost.
Read the Routing set to message.
Send a prompt and compare the chosen model with Expected.

S79.08.note: Local mode is the privacy setting; the zero-retention route option is not shown as a separate control.
steps: Type /privacy-settings and read the current mode and its description.
Type /privacy-mode local.
Type /privacy-settings again and confirm the mode is local.
Send a prompt and check that no cloud model name appears as the route, to compare with Expected.

S79.09.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account with /route auto set
S79.09.note: The intent classification itself has no control; the notice appears only when the chosen model changes.
steps: Use a managed cloud Auto session (/route auto) and send a coding question, then a plain chat question.
Look for an Auto route: notice in the chat when the model changes between the two messages.
S79.09.where: Inner behaviour: each message is classified by intent; the effect shows as an Auto route notice when the model changes

S79.10.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account with /route auto set
S79.10.note: No separate control exists; the tool classification is applied to the request without a visible setting.
steps: In a managed Auto session, ask for a task that needs tools (for example a file or search action).
Look for an Auto route: notice in the chat, and compare the model with a plain chat question.
S79.10.where: Inner behaviour: tool needs change the routing task; the effect shows as an Auto route notice

S79.11.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account with /route auto set, and an image file to attach
S79.11.note: The routing rule is in the classifier; no screen names image routing directly.
steps: In a managed Auto session, attach an image and ask a question about it.
Look for an Auto route: notice showing a different model than for a text-only question.
S79.11.where: Inner behaviour: attached images route the request to a multimodal model; the effect shows as an Auto route notice

S79.12.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account with /route auto set
S79.12.note: Effort classification is not shown as its own control.
steps: In a managed Auto session, send a simple greeting, then a long multi-step analysis request.
Compare the model named by any Auto route notice with Expected: the harder request should not drop to a weaker model.
S79.12.where: Inner behaviour: request complexity sets a quality floor; the effect shows as the model in an Auto route notice

S79.13.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account with /route auto set
S79.13.note: No separate freshness control was found; the search step itself is not confirmed on screen.
steps: In a managed Auto session, ask for today's news or a current price.
Look for an Auto route: notice or a search-related reply, and compare with Expected.
S79.13.where: Inner behaviour: current-information requests are detected and sent to search-capable handling; the effect is visible only through the routing notice

S79.14.needs: a Free account (so some models are locked)
S79.14.note: The lock annotation text was not found as a visible string; only a code comment describes it.
steps: Type /model to open the picker.
Look for model rows marked as locked or unavailable for the current plan, and compare with Expected: they are listed but cannot be used.
S79.14.where: Inner behaviour: ineligible models are filtered out before ranking; locked rows show in the /model picker

S79.15.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account with /route auto set
S79.15.note: The route ranking lives in the server-side auto routing; the visible output shows only provider and model.
steps: Run an Auto session and send a prompt.
Look for the Auto route notice, which names the provider and model used.
S79.15.where: Inner behaviour: one provider route is picked by health, cost and cache; no screen names the chosen route

S79.16.note: Fallback chains from -m a,b,c can still move a request to another model when the primary fails (see S79.20).
steps: Type /model and pick one specific model, then type a message.
Look for the Switched to line and check that no Auto route notice names a different model.
S79.16.where: Inner behaviour: a model chosen with /model is not swapped; the effect shows as no Auto route notice

S79.17.needs: credentials for the chosen provider, or a local Ollama install for ollama
S79.17.note: A provider lock setting beyond this flag was not found in the code.
steps: Start the CLI with agi --provider anthropic (or openai, google, ollama) plus --model for a model on that provider.
Type a prompt.
Check the banner line showing the model and provider, and compare with Expected.

S79.19.needs: a signed-in account with some usage
S79.19.note: The budget-aware route choice is applied on the server; the code path was not confirmed from the CLI side.
steps: Check your remaining usage with /usage or agi usage.
Send a prompt in an Auto session and compare the model with Expected.
S79.19.where: Inner behaviour: remaining budget is considered when choosing a route; no control shows it

labels.text: No fallback chain set. Restart with `--fallback-model <model>` or `-m a,b,c`.

S79.20.note: Demotion of unhealthy routes is not shown on screen; only the chain is visible.
steps: Start the CLI with agi --fallback-model <model> (or -m primary,backup).
Type /fallback and read the Fallback chain line.
Compare with Expected: when the primary fails, the reply names the backup model.

S79.21.needs: a Free account (a model outside the plan)
S79.21.note: The offer is a typed command in the message, not a one-click button; no one-click control was found.
steps: Choose a model your plan does not include, such as one the error names as unavailable.
Read the error text that appears in the chat.
Compare with Expected: the text suggests a switch command, which you type yourself.
S79.21.where: Shown in the error text when a model is unavailable, for example: Switch to ... with /model <name>

S79.23.note: Agent definitions take an optional model field (apps/cli/src/agents.rs); the exact view of the agent's model was not confirmed.
steps: Type /agents and read the list of agents.
Open an agent definition that has a model field, or run a task that uses that agent.
Compare the model shown for that agent with Expected: the worker should use its own model.

S79.26.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account and session saving on
S79.26.note: The notice shows only when the model changes; it does not explain why.
steps: Start with a managed cloud account and session saving on.
Type /route auto.
Send prompts of different kinds (a coding question, then a plain chat question).
Look for the Auto route: notice that names the route when the model changes, and compare with Expected.
S79.26.where: /route auto, then send a prompt and read the Auto route notice

S79.27.note: The banner at startup shows the model and provider (apps/cli/src/output.rs), and the Auto route notice names the model on change; no per-answer model label was found.

S79.28.note: The routing policy version is stored with the saved session (apps/cli/src/platform/runtime/session.rs), but no screen or command that displays it was found in apps/cli.

labels.text: Routing: off. Every message goes to

S79.30.needs: a signed-in managed cloud account with /route auto set
S79.30.note: Behaviour is in code (apps/cli/src/agent/chat.rs re_resolve_auto_route_for_turn); the failure itself is hard to trigger on demand.
steps: In a managed Auto session, send a prompt that is hard to classify (for example one short ambiguous word).
Check the reply still arrives and no Auto route notice appears.
S79.30.where: Inner behaviour: when routing classification fails, the current model is kept and the turn still runs; the effect shows as no error and the model staying the same
